question: In the waterfall model, when is a working system first delivered to the customer?
option_a: After the requirements phase, before design
option_b: After the whole sequence of phases, near the end
explanation: Picture building a branch in usable slices the customer can already use, or holding the whole building until the end: Waterfall completes requirements, design, implementation, and test in sequence, so the customer sees a working system late. Iterative models deliver slices earlier. Remember: late delivery of the whole product is the waterfall risk.
hint: Picture building a branch in usable slices the customer can already use, or holding the whole building until the end. Waterfall finishes one phase before it starts the next, and coding is not the first phase.
hint_2: Check the ideas that do not fit. A weekly working slice is an iterative idea. Delivery does not happen before requirements, and requirements alone are not a working system.
hint_3: The line to carry into the exam is this: late delivery of the whole product is the waterfall risk.

question: A black-box test is designed from which information?
option_a: The source code and every branch
option_d: The specification of inputs and expected outputs
explanation: Picture a closed box, where you may use the form's instructions but you may not open the machinery: Black-box testing treats the program as a closed box and chooses cases from the requirements, not from internal branches. White-box testing uses the code structure. Remember: if you do not look inside, it is black-box.
hint: Picture a closed box, where you may use the form's instructions but you may not open the machinery. The tester is not allowed to look inside the program.
hint_2: Check the ideas that do not fit. Branches, complexity, and object code are inside the box. Those belong to white-box thinking.
hint_3: The line to carry into the exam is this: if you do not look inside, it is black-box.

question: Cyclomatic complexity of a single connected flow graph, with E edges and N nodes, is given by which formula?
explanation: McCabe's number estimates how many independent paths the tests should cover. For one connected flow graph it is the number of edges, minus the number of nodes, plus 2. Remember: edges minus nodes plus 2.
hint: Adding edges and nodes moves the wrong way.
hint_2: A ratio of edges to nodes is not the formula.
hint_3: Subtract the nodes from the edges, then add 2.

question: Which coupling is the least desirable among these choices?
option_a: Data coupling through a short parameter list
option_d: Data coupling that passes only the values a callee needs
explanation: Content coupling means one module reaches into the private insides of another, so a small change can break the caller. Passing only the needed values is the loosest common form. Remember: reaching inside another module is content coupling.
hint: Passing simple values is the loose, desirable form.
hint_2: Passing a whole structure is tighter, but it is not the worst here.
hint_3: Reaching into another module's private data is the bad case.

question: In basic COCOMO, which project class assumes a small familiar team and stable, well-understood requirements?
option_c: Semidetached, but only when the product is a real-time kernel
option_d: Agile, which is a COCOMO mode
explanation: Picture a small familiar team estimating a job they already understand: Organic mode is the simple, well-understood end of basic COCOMO, while embedded mode is the tight, complex end. Semidetached sits between them. Remember: familiar and small means organic.
hint: Picture a small familiar team estimating a job they already understand. Basic COCOMO has three modes. The hardest constraints are not this mode.
hint_2: Check the ideas that do not fit. Embedded is the tight, complex end. Semidetached sits in the middle and is not limited to a kernel. Agile is not a COCOMO mode.
hint_3: The line to carry into the exam is this: familiar and small means organic.

question: A module has high cohesion when which of the following is true?
option_a: It performs many unrelated jobs so callers need only one module
option_b: It shares global data with every other module
option_d: Its elements all contribute to one well-defined task
explanation: Cohesion asks how focused a module is, not how many callers it has. High cohesion means every part of the module serves one clear job. Remember: one clear job means high cohesion, and many unrelated jobs means low cohesion.
hint: Packing unrelated jobs into one module lowers cohesion.
hint_2: Shared global data is a coupling problem, and a short file name does not measure cohesion.
hint_3: Every part contributes to one well-defined task.

question: Which testing level checks whether separately tested modules work together?
option_c: Acceptance testing by the end user only
explanation: Picture joining two modules that were each tested alone, to see whether the join holds: Unit testing exercises one module, and integration testing looks for interface faults when modules are combined. Acceptance testing asks whether the system meets the user's needs. Remember: the join between modules is integration testing.
hint: Picture joining two modules that were each tested alone, to see whether the join holds. Each module has already passed its own test. The new faults are at the joins.
hint_2: Check the ideas that do not fit. Unit testing exercises one module. Acceptance testing asks whether the whole system meets the user's needs. A rack test is not the software join.
hint_3: The line to carry into the exam is this: the join between modules is integration testing.

question: In a use-case diagram, an actor represents which of the following?
option_a: A Java class inside the system
option_c: A role played by a user or an external system that interacts with the system
explanation: Picture a stick figure standing outside the system and using it: An actor is outside the system boundary and starts or participates in a use case. It is a role, so one person may play several actors. Remember: outside the boundary, playing a role, means an actor.
hint: Picture a stick figure standing outside the system and using it. The stick figure stands outside the system boundary.
hint_2: Check the ideas that do not fit. A class, an index, and a line of code are inside the build. An actor is not those things.
hint_3: The line to carry into the exam is this: outside the boundary, playing a role, means an actor.
